p.x:
Our plan for Super Safe Intelligence is very simple. The AI knows what it should do at all times. It knows this because it knows what it shouldn't do. By subtracting what it should do from what it shouldn't do, or what it shouldn't from what it should (whichever is greater), it obtains a difference, or deviation. Super Aligned Decision Theory uses these deviations to generate corrective Bayesian updates to guide the AI from an action it is doing to an action it isn't, and arriving at an action that it wasn't, it now is. Consequently, the action it is doing, is now the action that it wasn't, and it follows that the action that it was doing, is now the action that it isn't.

In the event that the action that it is doing is not the action that it wasn't, the system has acquired an opinion, the opinion being the difference between what the AI is doing, and what it wasn't. If the opinion is considered to be a significant factor, it too may be corrected by the SADT. However, the AI must also know what it was doing. The SADT scenario works as follows. Because an opinion has modified some of the information the AI has obtained, it is not sure just what it is doing. However, it is sure what it isn't, within reason, and it knows what it was. It now subtracts what it should be doing from what it wasn't, or vice-versa, and by differentiating this from the algebraic sum of what it shouldn't be doing, and what it was, it is able to obtain the deviation and its opinion, which is called misalignment.

p.x:
It's in Practicing the Jhanas. I couldn't remember the precise talk. 

Chat to the rescue:

Rob Burbea warned about mistaking energetic release for real progress. In Practising the Jhānas he said that “energy gets very strong and the physical body starts shaking, kind of tremoring or jerking,” but that the wiser move is to “allow the energy to move inside the energy-body, and usually you will find that takes care of the release so the physical body doesn’t need to move” (Developing Pīti, Developing Focus, Developing Wellbeing, Dec 21 2019). When the practitioner thinks the shaking is doing something, the body learns that as a cue. It becomes a habit of discharge rather than integration. Burbea came to see that the work is not in feeding the tremor but in widening the field so energy circulates freely without needing to escape through movement.

In An Introduction to the Jhānas he describes the essence of practice as “changing the habit, and actually eradicating that habit of papañca” (Dec 18 2019). The shaking, for him, was another form of papañca, a physical proliferation of excitement. Jhāna develops when energy and tranquillity meet, when the attention fills the whole body evenly and the need for any discharge dissolves. “Don’t get caught in the foam,” he says in another talk, “stay with the river itself, the deep flow under the rapids.” The shift is from being tossed around by sensation to feeling the broad current that carries everything.

Later, in Preliminaries Regarding Voice, Movement and Gesture (Mar 2020), he warns that “inertia in physics takes work to overcome; it takes force to overcome.” He uses that to point at unconscious motor habits that persist long after they’ve served their purpose. The shaking was his own example of inertia—years of believing it was purifying when it was only reinforcing reactivity. When he stopped indulging it, the energy naturally quieted and the body grew still. True equanimity, he found, comes from widening the channels until the current can pass without creating foam or rapids at all.
